newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Feb 5.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Feb 5.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
FINANCIAL TIMES
-- TUBE SELL-OFF MIGHT HAVE TO BE FINANCED, PM TOLD

A leaked memo, from Transport Secretary Sir George Young to Prime Minister John Major, reveals that the proposed privatisation of the London Underground could end up costing the taxpayer money. In the memo, Sir George estimates that proceeds from the sell-off could be 1.2 billion stg to two billion stg. However, because an additional subsidy would have to be paid to eliminate an investment backlog, the sale could end up with the Treasury, as underwriter, having to make up a shortfall between the subsidy and the net proceeds.
-- RAILTRACK FREIGHT CODE SOUGHT

The Rail Freight Group, an industry body representing rail freight operators, is pressing for a code of practice to cover Railtrack's dealings with its customers, suppliers and others in the railway industry. The move follows what the operators see as foot-dragging by Railtrack over attempts to develop traffic and freight terminals. Among the group's demands are a commitment from Railtrack to targets for increasing freight and higher levels of investment.
-- DORRELL EXPECTED TO RELENT ON GPS

Health secretary Stephen Dorrell is expected later this month to relent on proposals in the government's NHS primary care bill, and rule out the possibility of commercial organisations such as chemists and supermarkets directly employing doctors. A number of supermarkets, as well as the pharmacy chain Unichem, have expressed an interest in contracting to hold general practice surgeries on their premises should the bill allow it. Dorrell has been put under pressure from the medical profession to curb the commercialisation of general practitioner services contained in the bill. -- CARMAKERS DISMISS CRASH TESTS AS 'SENSATIONALIST'

Motor manufacturers have criticised an attempt by the UK Department of Transport and a number of consumer bodies to introduce a new European standard car assessment programme. The new crash tests showed that many leading small cars performed poorly in frontal and side impact tests. However, car makers attacked the results as sensationalist and deliberately biased to show poor results.
-- MITSUBISHI LOOKS AT EUROPE EXPANSION

Japanese vehicle manufacturer Mitsubishi is reported to be considering plans for European expansion beyond its declared sales target of 330,000 units by the end of the decade. Mitsubishi is thought to be looking at expanding its Nedcar joint venture with Volvo in the Netherlands, which currently builds 200,000 cars and estates a year. The plant is due to get an assembly line to build 50,000 MGX vehicles a year, but the latest expansion plans may involve production of a third - so far unidentified - Mitsubishi model.
-- C&W AND VEBA FAIL TO REACH DEAL

UK telecoms group Cable & Wireless has failed to reach an early agreement with German industrial group Veba over dissolving their planned German telecoms alliance. It is understood that a disagreement over the amount Veba will pay C&W to buy its 45 per cent in their Vebacom joint venture is the stumbling block, although both sides are said to favour a speedy and amicable resolution. C&W has pulled out of the German alliance in order to concentrate its resources on the U.K. and Asian markets.
-- FREEPAGES TO RAISE CAPITAL VIA 'BOOK BUILDING'

Freepages Group, the Aim-listed classified telephone directory service, has become the first company in recent years to seek new capital through the U.S. practice of 'book building'. The move to book-building follows pressure from the Office of Fair Trading for shareholders in U.K. companies to accept greater competition in issue underwriting. Freepages, the competitor to British Telecom's Talking Pages service, is looking to raise 40 million stg to help fund a number of joint ventures.
-- KLEINWORT BANKER APPOINTED TI GROUP FINANCE DIRECTOR

Engineering and aerospace equipment specialist TI Group has announced the appointment of Martin Angle, a director at investment bank Kleinwort Benson, as its new finance director. The move is the first time in recent years that a FTSE 100 company has recruited a finance director from a City investment bank. Shares in TI fell 11.5p to 542.1p on news of the resignation for personal reasons of Brian Walsh, the current finance director.
-- STRONG GROWTH SHOWN BY BELL CABLEMEDIA

Cable company Bell Cablemedia has reported strong growth in revenues and customer numbers for 1996. Bell, the U.K.'s second largest cable company since its absorption of Videotron, said it added 20,294 cable TV customers, 20,457 residential telephony lines and 3,125 business telephony lines. However, net losses during the year increased from 47.4 million stg to 95.7 million stg, largely due to increased interest as well as the continuing costs of constructing the company's networks.
-- GULF BID OF 120P VIEWED AS 'INADEQUATE'

A increased offer of 120p a share from Gulf Canada Resources for U.K. independent oil group Clyde Petroleum has been described as 'inadequate' by one of the five institutions which control Clyde. The increased Gulf offer, up from its previous bid of 105p a share, was widely expected by oil industry analysts; it values Clyde at 494 million stg.
